en: Re-engraved Preface to the *Fǎmén Chújǐu* (and the *Wǔjiā Biànzhèng*) by Zhònggōng:
Zhònggōng pointed to the bandits of the Green Forest and called them "gentlemen who climb over beams. Who would have thought that within our Dharma-gate such a scoundrel could find a place?
Now that Master Fú of Báiyán has produced this compilation, long-standing rascals and ancient parasites will have no place to set foot.
Although various structures such as the lamp of ritual adornment and the lamp of meditation may be elaborately constructed, they are not worth even a single pinch [of dust].
This is why the "city of the sea" and the "mirage" appear in great abundance; yet when the bright sun shines beautifully across the heavens, they all vanish into nothingness.

Recently, constrained by my obligations, I composed the *Discrimination and Rectification of the Five Houses*. Regarding its words, whether they were clumsy or skillful, I could not help but perceive differences therein.
Since their meanings happen to converge upon a single principle, I have forgotten the shame of following like a dog’s tail after a pheasant’s plume;
I merely offer the sound of a single foot-long sword-ring, intended as a mere prelude to proclaim the true doctrine and rectify errors.
Preface to the *Famen chuji* (The Weeding of the Dharma Gate),
inscribed by the monk Cunde Yan on a day of the month of Guxiang in the spring of the Gengwu year of the Genroku era.

During the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, the monk Qing of Tiantai in Yue re-carved the *Dengyuan huoyuan* compiled by Dachuang. Yin Tingjun’s preface and introduction appended spurious remarks as minor annotations beneath the section on Emperor Tenmu.

Subsequent generations failed to discern their falsity and consequently accepted them as truth; this is much like regarding the Yin clan as the Minister of Justice or treating [the Emperor] as one who concealed his mother—it has been so for centuries. [Note:

The text provided appears to be a fragment from a historical or philological critique concerning the authenticity of certain records in Japanese Buddhist historiography (specifically the *Shoku Nihongi* or related works), referencing the work of the Chinese monk Dachuang and the commentary of Yin Tingjun.]

Until now, no one had been able to decide which version was correct. Now, the Venerable Baiyan of Qiantang has examined them through a chronological arrangement and traced them back to their origins through reason and circumstance.
Thus, the true and the false have been scrutinized, and the confusions and errors have been distinguished. To strip away the dense darkness and behold the sun—how remarkably clear this is!
From this day forward, regarding the two ancestral lineages of Yunmen and Fayan, people shall not dare to arbitrarily distort them by pulling this way or that.

Excellent! Your kindness toward future students is indeed consummate. I have therefore specially carved this into woodblocks to publish it for the world, so that not only may people know that Qiu Xuansu’s account is baseless, but also that Zhang Wujin certainly never saw the inscription by Jinshan Ying.
Thus, the arguments regarding the two inscriptions can surely be refuted once and for all.
There is nothing left to add; I shall not further indulge in redundant words.
Written by the abbot of Yunmen Xiansheng Chan Monastery, Daoist Ziru Shen, on the third day before the winter solstice in the eighth year of the Kangxi era (Jiyou), in the Baoming Hall.
*Fǎmén Chǔjiǔ*, Scroll One.
Written by the White Rock Odd Man of Ancient Hangzhou, Jìngfú;
reviewed by the Great Chū of Yuezhou Yunmen, Jìngshēn.
Below Nanquan there was a single Chan master named Tanzhao, who was a fellow brother in the Dharma with the elders Zhaozhou, Changsha, Zhuyou, and Zihu.
He resided at Baima in Jingzhou, and his realization transcended ordinary sentiment; his deeds were admirable. He would often say, "What joy! What joy!
yet when he approached his death, he cried out, "Suffering! Suffering! A head monk asked him about this, whereupon he pushed away his pillow.
The *pien* (chapters) and the *jiyu* (pith sayings) are fully recorded in the Imperial Collection (*huangzang*) and various *chuandeng* (transmission of the lamp) records.

Furthermore, both Dizang En and Baofeng Zhao have composed verses on them, which are currently carved and included in the *Songgu Lianzhu Ji* (Anthology of Linked Verses on Ancient Cases). These are things witnessed by all people throughout the world, past and present.

Yet modern people, driven by mere curiosity, construct towers and pavilions within empty space; they do not follow the actual reality, but instead— [The text continues: ...upon [the aforementioned works]. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Chan literature. The translation reflects the available portion.)
Mazu manifested the phantom of Tianwang Wulu, who then took the words of Tanzhao’s kōan and fashioned them into the deeds of Tianwang Wulu.
Thus, from beginning to end, not a single word was omitted and not a single character was altered; this is indeed a marvel. Alas!
How could there truly be two people in the same prefecture, sharing the same kōan and the same deeds? Is this not contrary to reason? Furthermore—
There was a person who re-engraved the *Denglu* (Record of Lamps), yet he went so far as to excise Bai Ma Tan Zhao outright.
By doing so, he caused the direct successor under Nanquan to vanish, leaving the generation of "dragon elephants" at Bai Ma to be heard of only in silence.
Furthermore, he inserted a spurious successor under Mazu, causing his one hundred and thirty-seven fellow disciples to remain in utter ignorance of him. What was his purpose?
Is it indeed so? I cannot know for certain; let me inquire of those with clear vision.
The fourth fascicle of the *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha), at the end of the chapter on Xuansha, states: "The lineage of Shitou reached this point and was thus revived.
Now, Xuansha and Yunmen were brothers, both of whom inherited from Xuefeng Cun. Cun, in turn, inherited from Deshan Jian.
Jian succeeded Longtan Xun; Xun succeeded Tianhuang Wu; Wu succeeded Shitou Xiqian. Juefan said, "The lineage of Shitou reached its resurgence at this point.
How could this have occurred without a broad foundation? Yunmen Wenyan emerged from Xianglin Chengyuan;
Chengyuan emerged from Zhimen Zuxiu; Zuxiu emerged from Xuedou Chongxian. This, moreover, is the most clearly established of the genealogical lineages.
The author writes: Water has its source; wood has its root. These are things that cannot be confused, for they are what they have come from.
Why is it that today there is no root, yet the stream flows so stubbornly? To falsely claim that [Xian] is the ninth-generation descendant of Da Ji—what kind of talk is this?
Alas! The Dharma-gate is in its autumnal decline; I did not expect it to reach such a state.
The *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records one hundred and thirty-eight successors of Mazu;
of these, seventy-five are included in the record, while sixty-three are not recorded because they lack recorded机缘 (ji-yuan) or dialogues.
This is consistent with what is recorded in the *Chuanfa Zhengzong Ji*. Initially, there was no mention of anyone known as "Tianwang Wu. The *Wudeng Huiyuan* records Mazu...
Seventy-six successors of Mazu are recorded; the *Zhizhuyulu* (Record of Pointing at the Moon) records forty-seven successors of Mazu.
In neither case is there anyone named "Tianwang Wu"; rather, the one recorded is "Tianhuang Wu.
Wu was a successor of Shitou Xiqian, representing the third generation of Qingyuan. The record states: "The third generation after Dajian [Huineng] was Shitou Xi..."
Master Qian Chan had twenty-one dharma heirs in total. The first was none other than Tianhuang Daowu of Jingzhou.

The *Chuan Deng Zheng Zong* (The Orthodox Lineage of the Lamp Transmission) is a canon preserved by successive dynasties; it is the family genealogy personally compiled by the direct sons and grandsons of this very school.
Other works include the *Xuefeng Guang Lu* (Extensive Record of Xuefeng), the *Lianzhu Tongji* (Comprehensive Collection of Linked Pearls), and the *Fozu* [Tongji].
Comprehensive records and essential collections have gathered many books. Who would not say that the lineage of Longtan originated from Qingyuan?
From the Tang dynasty down to the Qing, how many successive reigns have there been? How many times have these texts been perused by sage emperors and worthy ministers?
And how many times have the descendants of this lineage revered and honored them? For over a thousand years...
From of old, it has never been heard that anyone dared to arbitrarily move or alter it. For the source of water and the root of wood cannot be borrowed from elsewhere.
A Buddhist of the country of Bai said: "Seeing a stone at the summit of Mount Nanyue, he immediately returned to the ancient shore to consort with the sand gulls;
in vain did he divide the Hu-bread into fragrant bait, only to draw the golden dragon straight onto the hook. Reading this, one may also [attain realization].

It is perfectly clear; there is no further room for doubt. Why do people today not rely on the facts, but instead indulge their own whims to distort and confuse the truth, willingly falling into the ranks of the deluded and mediocre?
They have ultimately altered the lineage of Longtan to place it under Mazu’s assembly.
Furthermore, they have fabricated a "Tianwang Daowu" under Mazu, claiming he was a contemporary of Tianhuang Daowu in order to conflate them. Since this is already painfully baseless...
What is known as "words of karmic conditions" is actually a fabrication based on the episode of Nanyuan’s successor, Bai Ma Tan Zhao—
who reportedly said he was "happy" while alive but cried out in agony at the moment of death— which has been grafted onto the story of Tianwang’s enlightenment. Furthermore,
the name of the layman Li Mei of Haiyan was falsely assumed to conceal this transgression, and it was openly proclaimed in writing as the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings" and circulated.

The world looks down upon the Imperial Canon with contempt and does not fear the punishment of Heaven. Alas! Those who have left the household life do so for the sake of ending birth and death; what they value is that all things be true. To act with such deluded intentions—what is it that you hope to achieve?

Now, the compiler of the *Chuan Deng Lu* was the second-generation descendant of Dao Yuan and Fa Yan, while the author of the *Zheng Zong Ji* was the fourth-generation descendant of Ming Jiao and Yun Men.

Together they... [The Dragon]... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a historical or sectarian preface concerning the transmission of Chan Buddhism, likely from the Song dynasty. The final character "總" (zǒng) suggests the sentence continues, but as the source ends there, the translation reflects the available portion.)
Tan was the seventh-generation descendant. One cannot trust the family genealogy established by his own legitimate son and grandson; can anything outside of this be trusted?
Alas! The true shall not be suppressed, and the false shall not flourish. If the false were able to flourish, then I would consider these words of mine to be likewise spurious.
Chan Master Chongxin of Longtan in Lizhou was a native of Zhugong. His family made their living by selling cakes. From his youth, he was exceptionally gifted.
When the Master first attained enlightenment, the Venerable Heshang (Wuxue) secretly requested him to reside at Tianhuang Temple; no one could fathom his purpose.

The Master lived in the lane adjacent to the temple and would regularly send ten cakes to him every day (and so forth). This is recorded in various texts, including the *Fozu Tongji*, the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, and the *Zongmen Tongyao Xuanshe Huizuan*.
It is thus. As for the one who made a secret plea to the spiritual mirror, he was none other than Chengdong Tianhuang Daowu;
it is clear that this was not a fabricated "Daowu of the West. As for those who dwell in the temple lane, it refers to the temple lane of Chengdong Tianhuang Temple.
Today, there is a street called Tenno-koji (Heavenly Emperor Lane) to the east of the southern wall of Jingzhou; it is not something that can be erased from history.
Since the streets to the west of the city lack any name associated with a Heavenly Emperor, it is further evident that Longtan was not a successor to the Heavenly King.
Now, although these deluded people have carved out the mention of the Master Chuwu as Lingjian’s secret request for him to reside at Tenno-ji in the chapter on Longtan, [the truth remains].
The seventeen characters, "No one can fathom him," refer to the well-documented incident of his residence in the temple lane and his receipt of steamed buns;
these facts are so orderly and clear that they cannot be obscured. Why is this? It is because those who daily provided ten buns were offering them to Tianwang Daowu of the eastern city;
it was Tianwang Daowu who remained and returned the favor with buns. Thus, it is further clarified that he was not Tiantai Daowu.
Why is this? It is because his spiritual discernment was invoked in secret; as people could not fathom it, they were able to increase their offerings of ten cakes daily.

If it were as stated on the tombstone—that the Regional Inspector personally came to the prefectural office to welcome him and provide for his needs—then the four requisites would have been so abundant that even those of noble rank and high status could not obtain an audience, let alone a common shopkeeper daring to trouble him with ten cakes. As for people today...

Without careful examination, you have acted with a single-minded recklessness, indulging the mind of arising and ceasing to arbitrarily alter and change [the teachings], thereby throwing the ancestral lineage into disorder;
you have achieved nothing but the laughter of those who truly understand. Furthermore, what benefit or harm has this done to the other two schools, Yunmen and Fayan?
Moreover, when one hears of the epitaphs for Guifeng written by Zhang Jiuling and the inscription by Li Deyu, on what basis do they say such things?

Since there is no definitive evidence for such chronological deliberations, it goes without saying that they must have been fabricated with deceitful intent by those seeking to promote their own interests.
The *Preface to the Re-edited Lineage of the Five Houses* by Mengjue Tang states: "Zhang Wujin doubted [the authenticity of] Dongshan and Deshan..."
The manuscripts differ. I feared there might have been some error in the version from the Imperial Household.

Later, I obtained at the residence of Da’guan Ying (達觀頴) the "Epitaph for Emperor-Taoist Wu" (天皇道悟塔記) composed by Tang Fucai (符載), and I also recovered the "Epitaph for Heavenly King-Wu" (天王道悟塔記) written by Qiu Xuansu (丘玄素).
[These contain] such erroneous statements. When did Da’guan Ying pass away? Zhang Wujin (張無盡).
When did he pass away? Yet you say that Wu Jin obtained two inscriptions on the *Wu* stele from the place where [Da]ying was.
Now, Daguan Ying was the successor of Guyin Cong; he passed away on the eve of the New Year in the fourth year of the Jiayou era of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty, the Jihai year.
Zhang Wu Jin passed away in the eleventh month of the Sinxu year, the third year of the Xuanhe era of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty. Based on the Sinxu year...
Tracing back to the year Jihai (1619), sixty-three years have passed.

Even if he had lived to the age of seventy, he would have been only seven years old at the time of Master Ying’s passing; even if he had lived to eighty, he would have been no more than sixteen or seventeen.

This was precisely the period when he was studying for the civil service examinations, diligently occupied with literature and fame, and thus had no leisure for Buddhist studies. Yet, he found the leisure for them.
Indeed, even if one finds leisure for Buddhist studies, it does not necessarily mean one can apply oneself to the Chan school (zongcheng).

Even if one can apply oneself to the Chan school, it does not necessarily mean one can discuss the matters concerning its various gateways and lineages. How do we know this? According to the *Wujin zhuan* (Biography of Wujin): [text continues]
At the age of nineteen, while traveling to the capital to take the imperial examinations, he passed the state examination at the home of the Xiang family and subsequently became their son-in-law.

His first official appointment was as a District Magistrate (zhǔbù). Upon seeing the magnificent adornments of Buddhist scriptures, he was suddenly incensed and intended to compose a treatise denying the existence of the Buddha.

Later, while visiting his colleagues, he obtained a copy of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*; upon reading it, he was finally able to place his faith in the Buddha Vehicle. At that time, he was already over twenty years of age.
At more than twenty years of age, if one cannot even endure the sight of the majesty of the Buddhist scriptures (*braṇakṣepa*), then one has not yet given rise to faith in the Buddha-dharma.

If one has not yet given rise to faith, how could one possibly pay attention to the *yāna* of the ultimate truth (*zōngchéng*) or discuss matters concerning the various schools and lineages? This is merely stated with reference to a lifespan of eighty years; if...
Wujinshou died at seventy; thus, he must have been merely a child of one hundred and sixty-seven years old before Ying passed away.
Yet, [the author] claims to have obtained a stele inscription for Fu Zai from Ying, and furthermore to have sought out a stele inscription for Qiu Xuansu.
Is this so, or not? This does not require further debate to be understood by oneself; it is clear that these accounts are spurious and exaggerated. Moreover, Wujin was preoccupied with...

The core teaching was realized during his later years. According to the biography, in the sixth year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong (the Xinwei year), he served as the Grain Commissioner for Jiangxi.
There, he met Doushuai Yue; he harbored great doubt regarding the story of the alms-bowl. At midnight, he overturned a washbasin and thereby attained thorough enlightenment.
He was then fifty years of age. Counting back from the *xuwei* year of the Yuanyou era to the *jiahai* year of the Jiayou era, thirty-three years elapsed.

It was only then that he attained awakening to the *zongcheng* (the vehicle of the lineage). How could it be that, even before having seen Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven, this youth was already suddenly able to maintain such a discourse on the matters of Dongshan and Deshan’s "reaching out their hands" to receive and guide sentient beings? Furthermore, regarding this maintained discourse, it is stated that now—
By verifying this with the two records of Qiu and Fu, one will finally know that my selection of the Dharma and examination of people were not mistaken;

thus, these words must have been written prior to the discovery of the stele. How could a scholar who had only been devoted to his studies for ten-odd years suddenly be able to produce such language concerning the inner sanctum of this vehicle of the school?
This would perhaps be slightly more credible if it were from someone who had already attained direct realization after seeing Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven.
If it is said that this occurred before Daoguan had attained stillness, then a child who is utterly ignorant could certainly not have reached such a state.
Furthermore, his family resided in Zhugong; Zhugong is located in Jingzhou.

Since there are already steles for both Tianhuang and Tianwang to the east and west of the city, Dao’wu alone—or perhaps two individuals—must have been present day and night before the Infinite Brow (Wujinmei).

Within the space between one's eyelashes, things are indeed clearly manifest; not even a hair’s breadth is obscured. Why, then, should you harbor doubts that there are two different people named Dao-wu?

And why must you offer the excuse that it was only after obtaining the two steles of Qiu and Fu from Da-guan that he finally gained self-confidence, proving his discernment and testing of men to be unerring?
Furthermore, Da-guan resided at Jin-shan, which is three thousand *li* away from Zhu-gong.
Furthermore, how could one fail to examine the steles right before one’s eyes, yet instead laboriously travel thousands of li from afar to seek them out?
What need is there to debate the falsity of such claims? This is merely a fabrication by later generations;
it is nothing more than groundless and empty delusion. To force a gentleman to believe in groundless and empty delusions is perverse.

Furthermore, what can be gained? My wish is that those who shoulder the burden of the Dharma-gate should uphold public integrity and maintain rectitude; it would suffice if they do not increase one's delusions.
During the Ming Chenghua and Hongzhi eras, there was Zen Master Xueting. He was the son of the Gui family of Guiyi, Hangzhou. He opened the Dharma at Zhaokong Temple and served as the Abbot of Linji.
Twenty-four generations later, there was the Master Xiuxiu of Zhizhi Hall in Western Sichuan, the son of Nanfeng. His *Huàn jì lù* (Record of Illusory Dwelling) circulates in the world;
however, the *Xù lìedēng* (Continued Abridged Lamp History) erroneously lists him among those of unknown lineage. This is an error.

Furthermore, in the *Gǔnán kèshī niān gǔ* (Ancient South’s Commentary on Old Cases), he is recorded under the name Gūtíng Qiánjiān; this likewise fails to recognize that [he was actually] Gūtíng Xuètíng.
How much more so when it concerns the lineage: Gu Tingjian was a direct successor of Wuji Wuzhu, whereas Xueting was separated from Wuzhu by two generations—namely Xuefeng Xiu and the Elder Huiguo.
Thus, Gu Ting and Xuefeng were brothers, and Xueting was a grandson of Gu Ting.
Why, then, have they been conflated into a single person? Alas! From Mingzhi to Qingliang there are merely two [generations].
Even the errors in the compilation of the *Baolin Zhuan* are as such; how much more so must this be the case for the period from the Tang dynasty to the present, spanning nearly a millennium?

Jiyin took the Heavenly Sovereign (*tennō*) and the Heavenly King (*tennō*) to be two different persons. Recently, they have gone so far as to treat the Heavenly Sovereign and the Heavenly King as distinct individuals.
It is only natural that there is no need to debate this; what reliance can be placed on a forged inscription?
*The Plowshare Investigation of the Dharma-gate* (with preface).
Once the "Plowshare Investigation" chapter was published, some remarked: "Among those who commit transgressions and incur resentment, none exceed those who are fond of speaking exhaustively.

Regarding the fluctuations between the superior and inferior [teachings] within the Dharma-gate, there already exist works such as *Correcting Errors*, *Extinguishing Deviance*, and *Relying on Reality*. Since the truth is already..."

It cannot be concealed. How, then, could falsehood ever flourish? Even if there were those who pointed to a deer as a horse or identified a tortoise as a turtle—such instances being rare—they would merely be venting their grievances and expressing their indignation.
Yet, this magnificent great nation abounds in clear-sighted, upright, and great gentlemen; how, then, could [falsehood] ever prevail over them all?
How deluded they are! A single hand is truly insufficient to shield the sun; it would be better to simply set them aside.
Furthermore, why such excessive injury to virtue and waste of words? I replied, "Indeed. How could I delight in speaking exhaustively? Yet there are circumstances that render it unavoidable.
For those in this world who advocate doctrines that harm [the truth] and serve as the source of confusing the authentic—such individuals..."
If a calamity affects only one person, it may not be necessary to investigate it; but if the calamity extends to all under heaven and to future generations, can its investigation be postponed?

If one is merely preoccupied with purifying oneself and maintaining a sense of integrity, avoiding arrows and fearing the blade, one will endure the eternal Way that has remained unchanging for a thousand ages.
Once one is mired in the darkness of ignorance, one will surely incur the censure of the world;
how could one avoid feeling shame before the Dharma Hall in future generations? This is precisely why I have acted as I have, out of absolute necessity.
Thus, how could it be that I delight in speaking exhaustively, thereby wounding my virtue with superfluous words?

How profound! Furthermore, I have heard it said that only those who are truly virtuous can receive exhaustive counsel. Thus, regarding Master Hui, how could I dare to treat him as one who is not virtuous?
It would be appropriate for me to speak exhaustively to him. Moreover, I have not yet spoken exhaustively, and this is because my purpose lies in defending the Way.
Written on the ninth day of the ninth month in the Dingwei year by the White Rock Occasional Practitioner, Jingfu.
Since the beginning of heaven and earth, there has been no era in which debate over right and wrong has been absent.

First, let the officials of the government, with clear vision and a great public mind, issue a supreme judgment of public righteousness: let the right be restored to its rightful place, and the wrong to its own. Once right and wrong are made manifest, debate will subside and cease.
We may then forget one another in the realm of the Lord of No-Thought (Wuhuai), each returning to our respective [natural state].

Rest assured in your life. Suppose in a future generation there should be a person who says, "What was right before can now be made wrong; what was wrong can now be made right. Thus, right and wrong are inverted;
public judgment is destroyed and the impartial mind is extinguished. Out of that which is inherently devoid of right and wrong, they falsely give rise to them.
They darken the sun and moon and throw the fundamental social order into chaos. Yet, the public offices still exist, and those with clear vision still exist—yet [they remain silent] until...
Your Excellency has debated this matter and cannot forget it. In our school during the Tang dynasty, there was a single master, Zen Master Tianhuang Daowu, who resided in Jiangling, Chu.
He was the disciple of Shitou Xiqian, and from his lineage emerged the two schools of Yunmen and Fayan.

These details are recorded most extensively in the Imperial Canon (*Daizō*), the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), and the *Zheng Zong Ji* (Record of the True Lineage). The compiler of the *Chuan Deng Lu* was Dao... [text fragment ends]
Yuan was the second-generation descendant of Fayan. Mingjiao Song authored the *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True Lineage); he was the fourth-generation descendant of Yunmen.
The genealogical succession of their respective lineages is meticulously organized, and its origins are ancient.

Although the *Huìyuán* contains minor characters or omissions of doubt, everyone knows these are errors; therefore, the carvers did not dare to transcribe them in large characters. This was done by later people.
Without basing themselves on the original sources, they have recklessly cited authorities to alter established terminology and disrupt the ancestral lineage.

Previously, great gentlemen of supreme integrity analyzed these errors until they were cleared away like melting ice; for many years now, the two schools have been able to each rest secure in their own traditions.
Now, the recklessness of Shuijian has suddenly emerged, and Huishan has further followed suit in fabricating associations, thereby defiling and profaning the Dharma-gate.
If one further confuses the ancestral lineage, how could one possibly avoid being subjected to debate?

Nevertheless, the insertion of small characters has become a matter of doubt, serving as a test for the wisdom or folly of those in future generations. Perhaps the intent of Master Haiqing may be commended;
we ourselves need not investigate it further. However, if later students are unfamiliar with this and successively treat it as fact, the harm to our school will not be small. Therefore—
We cannot help but report this. Please allow me to illustrate this with a recent example. Within the Linji lineage, there is currently one person who transmits the orthodox line:

Haizhou Ci. According to the *Fozu Yuanliu Gao* (Draft on the Genealogy of Buddhas and Patriarchs) produced by the Chai family of Suzhou during the Bingzi year of the Chongzhen era, it is stated that Ci was first the successor of Wanfeng Wei and later the successor of Dongming Xian. For this reason—

The two men shared a single successor. According to the *Stūpa Inscription* and the *Eulogy on the Seal* composed by Shen Guan, Wansong’s direct heir was Cui, who was a contemporary of Baozangchi, while Dongming was Cui’s dharma nephew.
According to the *Night Talks at the Guest Window* by Wuwen Cong, Cui was [the successor] of Wansong... [text fragment ends].
Wey’s disciple was the master of Baofeng Xuan. [The text] barely mentions Baozang Dongming and treats him as a later reappearance of the same name.

Furthermore, based on the memorial for Guxi, there is suspicion that beneath the name Dongming there may have been another person sharing the same name as Ci, similar to the case of the two Daowus of Jingnan and Liangdao.
Baohua, relying on Jing’an Su’s *Lianfang* (Flower Garland), [asserts...]
Regarding the chronological sequence and genealogical descriptions in the chart, it treats Ri (Ri Ji) as the son of Dongmyeong and the teacher of Bopong;
however, under Wanpung, there was another individual with the same name and title, Ri.
When Santsaigong himself recounted his time residing at Dongmyeong, he discovered an inscription for the stupa of Hyon-iam among discarded papers. This inscription contained no mention of Haewo.
Regarding the name "Maitreya," the five aforementioned accounts do not accord with one another.

Although there is no way to verify the original source or its branches and descendants, alas, it is a matter of barely more than two hundred years from past to present, yet few are even able to clarify it.

How much more so regarding the realization of the Two Paths (Dao) occurring over a thousand years ago, separated by ten dynasties and seventy-odd emperors? And yet, how is it that people of today alone [can know] this?
Should one report this? Indeed, from the perspective of realizing the One Way, taking two people as one is not impossible;
however, when examining historical records and verifying the chronology, the distinction between the authentic and the spurious cannot help but be discerned.
For instance, there are inscriptions fabricated by those fond of such things to curry favor with figures like Zhang Wujin, which claim [the stele] was from the Tang dynasty.
Composed by Qiu Xuansu, Grand Master of Discourses (Yi Dafu), Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue (Hubu Shilang), Chancellor (Pingzhangshi), and Regional Inspector of Jingnan (Jingnan Jiedushi).

Those who lack eyes have handed down this tradition as authentic; yet when one examines the historical records, annals, the chronological table of Tang Prime Ministers, and the local gazetteers of Jingzhou, it becomes clear that Qiu Xuansu is a mere non-entity, and the spurious nature of the inscription is as evident as the sun and moon.
Your Majesty may now be free from doubt. As the proverb goes: "When the hide no longer exists, the hair has no place to which it can adhere.

Since the error has been clarified, what further need is there to say? It is truly a blessing for the Dharma that the two houses of Ji and Dong have fortunately maintained peace and harmony over these years.

I did not expect that there would now suddenly appear one Seng Shuijian, who purchased the site of the residence of the scholar Kong Weiran at the Yilu Gate south of the city of Jingzhou and constructed a hermitage to dwell in.
Having carved out a void from nothingness, he gave it the name "Ancient Tianwang Temple," deceiving the ignorant and deluding the masses to the point of harming the truth.
